Pool service in Sahuarita, AZ, starts with a question many owners never think about: which of the area's seven water providers fills their pool. Add the Town's own steps for emptying a pool, two possible electric utilities and long summer heat, and a Sahuarita pool has its own checklist. This page walks through it.

First, what this site is. Tucson Pool Cleaning Pro has no crews and sells no pool work. Its number, (520) 372-1083, is answered by an automated assistant that asks about the pool, then sends the call to a locally owned, independent pool service company working in Sahuarita. That company does any inspection, quoting and work, and bills you itself.

Sahuarita: a ranch name, pecan groves and fast growth

Sahuarita became an incorporated town on September 20, 1994. The Town says it had about 1,800 residents then; the 2020 Census counted 34,134, up from 25,259 in 2010. The name traces to the Sahuarito Ranch, which operated here from 1879 to 1886, and is said to mean "little saguaro." The Santa Cruz River runs through the area, and the Town describes significant acreage of pecan groves running through it.

Two big communities shape a lot of the housing. Rancho Sahuarita is a master-planned community that an older Town economic development plan, from around 2008, described as planned for 11,680 homes. Quail Creek is an age-restricted community that the same plan put at about 5,000 homes, and a newer Quail Creek expansion is still moving through the Town's planning process. Census figures put roughly one resident in five at 65 or older, and about 81% of homes are owner occupied.

Seven water providers, one groundwater basin

The Town of Sahuarita does not sell water. Its water information page lists seven separate providers, and a Town study session on the area's water supply described the community as relying on groundwater. Which provider serves you depends on where your home sits, and this page will not guess for any neighborhood. Look at your water bill, then find that provider's annual water quality report for its hardness reading.

Why it matters for a pool: every inch the sun takes out of the pool leaves its dissolved minerals behind, and the next top-up adds more. The Arizona Department of Water Resources figures open water in the Tucson region loses around six feet a year. Calcium hardness, a measure of how much calcium is dissolved in the pool, builds up until it shows as a white crust at the tile line or a rough feel on the plaster. Testing it a few times a year tells you whether scale is on its way, and pool tile cleaning explains what can be done once the crust appears.

Emptying a pool the way the Town asks

Sahuarita is an incorporated town, and its wastewater FAQ spells out how pool water should leave a property. When high calcium or dissolved solids mean the water has to be changed, these are the Town's points.

Your own cleanout

Send the water through the access cap of the private sewer cleanout on your property. That is the discharge point the Town names.

Keep the flow in check

Throttle the pump so the private sewer line, called the lateral, does not back up and spill pool water onto your yard or the house next door.

Stay out of the street

Never open a public manhole or a cleanout in the street. The Town warns that it disrupts traffic and puts people walking by, children and neighbors at risk.

TEP or Trico, by address

Both electric utilities serve parts of Sahuarita. Trico Electric Cooperative has a Sahuarita board district, and Tucson Electric Power has a transmission project, the Santa Rita Connection, serving Sahuarita and Green Valley. Your bill tells you which one runs your pump. On TEP's time of use plans, summer weekday afternoons from 3 to 7 p.m. are on-peak, so a pump timer set for the morning keeps the long summer runs out of that window. Check your own plan before changing the schedule.

Monsoon season on the south side

The National Weather Service in Tucson counts June 15 through September 30 as monsoon season. Storm winds strip leaves and dust off the desert and drop them in the water, and big rains can raise the water level and thin out the chlorine. A quick look at the skimmer, the pump basket and a fresh water test after each storm saves trouble later.

  • Gate. Make sure the pool gate still swings shut and latches; the Town's building staff can explain local barrier rules.
  • Kids and grandkids. An adult should watch any child near the pool at every moment, and a pool without a fence or cover is off limits.
  • Gauge. Jot down the filter pressure when the pool is clean so you notice when it climbs.
  • Pad. Look for drips or puddles at the equipment, without opening any electrical box.
  • Products. Pool chemicals stay in their own labeled containers and are never combined. Keep them dry, out of the sun and locked up.

Gas smell near the heater? Get everyone away from it at once, and leave the heater, light switches and anything that could spark untouched. From a safe distance, call 911 and Southwest Gas at 877-860-6020.

Look up the contractor license. Contractor licensing in Arizona is handled by the state Registrar of Contractors, known as the ROC. A residential R-6 license, Swimming Pool Service and Repair, is the one meant for servicing home pools and making minor repairs; building a pool or replacing a whole plaster or pebble interior falls under construction licenses such as B-5. Whether a cleaning-only route needs any license is not spelled out by the ROC, so it is fair to ask a company what it holds. Write down its ROC number and enter it in the state's license lookup (new tab), which lists the license status, classification and recent complaints. Tucson Pool Cleaning Pro does not run this check on anyone.

Common questions

Is there pool service in Sahuarita, AZ, that I can call at night?

You can call the line at night. Dial (520) 372-1083 at 2 a.m. if you need to. An automated assistant picks up, writes down the trouble and that you live in Sahuarita, and connects you to a pool service company nearby that is independent and locally owned. Should nobody answer there, your details and a note on the pool are passed along for a return call. Any bill is between you and that company; the line charges nothing.

Who supplies water to my Sahuarita home?

The Town of Sahuarita does not run a water utility. The Town lists seven providers in the area: Sahuarita Water Company, Farmers Water Company, Quail Creek Water Company, Community Water Company of Green Valley, Las Quintas Serenas Water Company, Sahuarita Village Water and Valle Verde del Norte Water Cooperative. Your monthly water bill names the one that serves you.

How do I empty a pool in Sahuarita?

The Town's wastewater FAQ says to discharge through the access cap of the sewer cleanout on your own property, to control the flow so the private sewer line does not overflow onto your yard or a neighbor's, and never to use a public manhole or cleanout in the street. The Town also publishes Guidelines for Emptying a Pool with more detail.

Is Sahuarita water hard on a pool?

No published hardness figure for any of the seven Sahuarita-area providers turned up in our research, so this page does not give one. Your provider's annual water quality report is the place to look. Either way, a pool's calcium rises as water evaporates and is topped up, so ask for a calcium hardness test when the pool company visits.

Does Quail Creek or Rancho Sahuarita change who I call for pool service?

No. The same free number works anywhere in Sahuarita. If your community has an HOA, it may have its own rules about equipment placement, draining or yard work, so check them before a big job, and ask the pool company whether it has worked under similar rules.

It is one free call, day or night. Tell the assistant what the pool is doing and which part of the Tucson area it is in, and you are transferred to a local, independently owned pool company that looks at the pool in person and names its own price.
